To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
seasonal demand increases reduce the costs of informative advertising by retailers (and possibly manufacturers), which in turn allows for greater price sensitivity on behalf of buyers.

1) food prices decline seasonally; 2) price declines are not driven primarily by falling agricultural input costs; 3) price declines are driven by the fact that the effective costs of advertising fall at seasonal demand peaks; and 4) the fact that the costs of informative advertising fall at seasonal peaks leads to increased market information and price sensitivity on the side of buyers.

price declines at seasonal demand peaks are driven by the increased ability of buyers to identify low prices, which is in turn facilitated by increased informative advertising by manufacturers and retailers, and that these price declines are larger in competitive markets than in markets with a single dominant brand.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the demand for a seasonal product affects the price of that product and how that relationship is influenced by competition.
the role of competition in the food industry, and the implications for consumer welfare.
understanding how the demand for food products and the structure of the food retail industry affect the price paid for food.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
demand, information, and competition are all important determinants of seasonal food price declines.
the seasonal price declines are driven by competition, and not by the seasonality of the agricultural input costs, as the conventional wisdom would have it.
the price decline is not a function of the seasonal demand increase.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the market is not a zero sum game, and that the market can be a win-win situation for both producers and consumers.

the demand for seasonal products is more elastic than the supply, and that competition in the form of informative advertising and/or increased retailer and manufacturer competition is a key factor in explaining why prices for seasonal products fall when demand is highest.

the demand peaks of seasonal products provide an opportunity for retailers and manufacturers to increase market information, and that this increased information is a major factor driving seasonal price declines.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the market structure of the retail industry is an important determinant of the price declines observed in seasonal markets.
price declines at demand peaks are not driven by the same factors that drive price increases at demand troughs.
price declines at seasonal peaks may reflect a combination of market structure, information, and demand.
